title: Question 12
stem: The incomplete nuclear equation for one possible reaction that takes place in the core of a nuclear reactor is $$^{235}_{92}\text{U} + ^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow ^{139}_{57}\text{La} + ^{95}_{42}\text{Mo} + 2^{1}_{0}\text{n} + ................$$

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State the name given to this type of nuclear reaction.
hints: Hint 1: Look at what happens to the heavy uranium nucleus - it is hit by a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei, La and Mo. What is the name for splitting of a heavy nucleus?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recognise the Splitting Process**
A heavy nucleus like $^{235}_{92}\text{U}$ absorbs a neutron and then breaks into two medium-mass daughter nuclei, $^{139}_{57}\text{La}$ and $^{95}_{42}\text{Mo}$, plus a few neutrons. Splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei of comparable size is called nuclear fission. This is different from fusion where light nuclei join together.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Add up the top numbers (nucleon number $A$) on the left and on the known products on the right. What top number and bottom number must the missing particle have to keep both totals balanced?
Hint 2: The proton numbers do not balance - left side is 92 but La + Mo already give 99. What particle has $A = 0$ and $Z = -1$ that could remove the extra positive charge?
parts.proper_answer: Missing product is $7^{0}_{-1}e$ (seven beta-minus particles / electrons).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Balance the Nucleon Number $A$**
On the left: $$A = 235 + 1 = 236$$ On the right so far: $$A = 139 + 95 + 2 \times 1 = 236$$ The $A$ values already balance, so the missing product must have $A = 0$.

Step 2: **Balance the Proton Number $Z$**
On the left: $$Z = 92 + 0 = 92$$ On the right so far: $$Z = 57 + 42 + 2 \times 0 = 99$$ There are 7 extra protons on the right. To balance, the missing product must have total $Z = 92 - 99 = -7$ with $A = 0$. A particle with $^{0}_{-1}e$ is an electron or beta-minus particle. So you need 7 of them: $$^{235}_{92}\text{U} + ^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow ^{139}_{57}\text{La} + ^{95}_{42}\text{Mo} + 2^{1}_{0}\text{n} + 7^{0}_{-1}e$$

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: The mass defect for the reaction is $0.223\text{ u}$.
parts.text: Calculate the energy, in $\text{J}$, equivalent to $0.223\text{ u}$.
hints: Hint 1: The lost mass appears as energy via $E = mc^2$. First think how to change 0.223 u from unified atomic mass units into kilograms.
Hint 2: Use $1\text{ u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$ and $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\text{ m s}^{-1}$, then calculate $E = (\Delta m)c^2$ to get joules.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Convert Mass Defect to Kilograms**
Mass and energy are linked by Einstein's relation $E = mc^2$, but $m$ must be in $\text{kg}$. $$\Delta m = 0.223 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$$ $$\Delta m \approx 3.70 \times 10^{-28}\text{ kg}$$ This tiny lost mass is the source of the released energy.

Step 2: **Apply $E = mc^2$**
Now multiply by $c^2$: $$E = \Delta m c^2$$ $$E \approx (3.70 \times 10^{-28}) \times (3.00 \times 10^{8})^2$$ $$E \approx 3.3 \times 10^{-11}\text{ J}$$ This is the energy released per single fission reaction.

markscheme_points.text: kinetic energy of fission products (nuclei, neutrons, beta particles)

hints: Hint 1: After fission the products fly apart very fast - what form of energy does a fast-moving fission fragment or neutron carry?
Hint 2: As well as particles, fission releases high-frequency electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus - what is this penetrating photon called?
parts.proper_answer: 1. Kinetic energy of the fission products (La, Mo nuclei), neutrons and beta-particles. 2. Energy of gamma-ray photons.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Kinetic Energy of the Products**
The daughter nuclei, neutrons and electrons repel each other and fly apart at high speed. Much of the $3.3 \times 10^{-11}\text{ J}$ appears as kinetic energy of these particles. This random kinetic energy later becomes thermal energy in the reactor coolant.

Step 2: **Gamma Radiation**
The newly formed nuclei are often in excited states and de-excite by emitting high-energy photons. So a second form is electromagnetic energy as gamma-ray photons, with energy $E = hf$.
